title: Online scams drain over Rs 4 billion in three years as Nepal plans anti-scam center - myRepublica
description: Online scams drain over Rs 4 billion in three years as Nepal plans anti-scam center  myRepublica
publisher.title: myRepublica
full_article:
KATHMANDU, Oct 29: By the time victims report an online scam and police contact banks to freeze the stolen money, it is often too late. The funds have already moved, leaving victims with little chance of recovering their losses.

(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});

Now, the government is preparing to establish an integrated anti-scam center at the Cyber Bureau of Nepal Police, bringing banks, digital wallet operators and telecom service providers together to help stop fraudulent transactions before the money disappears.

The move comes as complaints filed with the bureau over the past three fiscal years involve more than Rs 4 billion in alleged scam-related losses. With online fraud becoming increasingly widespread, the bureau is also preparing to strengthen its infrastructure, technology and investigative capacity.

Currently operating from a narrow alley in Bhotahity, Kathmandu, the bureau is set to move to a new building in Samakhusi. The new facility will not only provide modern infrastructure and technology but also accommodate private-sector representatives who will work alongside police investigators.

Established in 2018 as a specialized unit to investigate cybercrime, the bureau receives more than 7,000 complaints annually, most involving online fraud. Online gambling scams, fake lottery messages and theft of money directly from bank accounts are among the most common cases.

Under the proposed arrangement, representatives from all 20 Class A commercial banks will work at the bureau in three shifts. A work procedure is being prepared to facilitate their deployment and ensure they can assist investigations.

Digital wallet operators eSewa and Khalti will also be required to assign representatives, while Nepal Telecom and internet service providers will deploy staff to cover all three shifts, according to Cyber Bureau chief Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Nabinda Aryal.

The plan envisages stationing 114 private-sector representatives at the bureau to support police investigations.

“Victims of cyber scams transfer money to bank accounts or digital wallets. Such transactions must be stopped immediately. By the time we write to banks and wallet companies requesting them to freeze the funds, it is often too late, leaving victims with little chance of recovering their money,” Aryal said.

“With representatives of banks and wallet companies stationed at the bureau, we can freeze the funds as soon as a complaint is received,” he added.

Many victims fall for messages claiming they have won a lottery and transfer money to accounts or digital wallets believing the offers are genuine. Others disclose their personal and banking details to callers posing as bank employees, sometimes losing their entire savings.

The accounts used to receive stolen money are often opened using citizenship documents belonging to people other than the actual perpetrators. Unless the funds are frozen quickly, recovering them becomes difficult, Aryal said.

Retired central bank employees among victims

Online scammers have targeted not only ordinary citizens but also former employees of Nepal Rastra Bank.

In a case filed about a month ago, scammers allegedly called retired central bank employees, claiming that their know-your-customer (KYC) details needed updating. The bureau investigated after the victims reported that money had been stolen from their bank accounts.

Thirty-nine former Nepal Rastra Bank employees filed complaints over the theft. An investigation found that Rs 17.9 million had been stolen. Police arrested four people in connection with the case, and three were remanded in custody pending trial.

The bureau has also helped victims recover Rs 4.9 million lost to online fraud and bank account theft.

According to police data, 2,379 complaints were filed over the past three fiscal years by people who lost money after trusting calls claiming that their bank or financial institution details needed updating or after disclosing their one-time passwords (OTPs).

These figures cover only complaints registered with the Cyber Bureau. In fiscal year 2025/26, the bureau received 7,296 cybercrime complaints, most of which involved financial losses.

Over the past three fiscal years, complaints involving more than Rs 4 billion in alleged scam-related losses have been registered with the bureau. Delays in coordinating with banks and financial institutions to freeze the funds have made it difficult to recover money for victims.

The proposed anti-scam center aims to address this gap by enabling faster coordination among investigators and financial service providers.

Police seek more than 1,000 cyber security personnel

Alongside the planned anti-scam center, Nepal Police is seeking to expand its cyber security workforce as part of its three-year plan.

The police have submitted a proposal to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking approval to recruit more than 1,000 personnel dedicated to cyber security. The proposal has also been forwarded to the Ministry of Finance, a Home Ministry official said.

Police Spokesperson DIG Abi Narayan Kafle said cyber units equipped with technical personnel had already been established at district police offices across the country. However, a shortage of skilled personnel has prompted the police to seek additional positions.

“Cybercrime control is the top priority in the inspector general's three-year action plan. The organization is working accordingly,” Kafle said.

“Efforts are underway to develop personnel capable of addressing risks posed by artificial intelligence and to strengthen the Cyber Bureau.”

title: Nepal-India Tourism Council to be set up - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal-India Tourism Council to be set up  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Chitwan, Oct 29: A council is being set up between Nepal and India to promote tourism, expand business relations, and jointly develop the tourism sector.

The 'Nepal–India Cross-Border Tourism Connect 2026' programme, jointly organized here from October 25 to 27, by the Non-Resident Nepali Association International Coordination Council and the Prosperous Chitwan Campaign, decided to increase the arrival of Indian tourists in Nepal, promote Nepali tourism in India, and develop long-term business partnerships between tourism entrepreneurs of both countries.

The proposed council will include tourism experts, travel and tour operators, hotel and resort managers, hospitality sector specialists, and other stakeholders from both countries.

The main objectives of the council will be joint destination promotion, B2B meetings, creating joint tourism packages, exchanging experiences, and running regular networking programmes.

During the programme, Nepalese hotel and resort operators and Indian travel and tour operators had B2B meetings, tourism networking, and professional interactions.

Somanath Sapkota, spokesperson of the Non-Resident Nepali Association International Coordination Council and chairman of the Tourism Promotion Committee, shared that there was a discussion on connecting Nepal's tourist destinations with the Indian market, creating joint tourism packages, exchanging experiences, and expanding regular business contacts.

According to him, the programme will help promote Nepal as an attractive destination for Indian tourists and create new opportunities for the tourism business.

Among the notable participants of the programme were Sharada Basyal, Executive Director of the Lumbini Province Tourism Promotion Council, Rajesh Singh, President of the Travel Trade Welfare Association of India, Dr. KP Singh, representative of the Indo-Nepal Tourism Welfare Society, and Robin Prasad Sherchan, Senior Vice President of the Non-Resident Nepali Association International Coordination Council.

As a part of the programme, the participants visited various tourist destinations, hotels, and resorts in Ramgram, Amaltari, Maulakalika, Sauraha, Meghauli, Chitwan, and Nawalpur.

The participants got information about the religious and historical significance of Ramgram, the Tharu culture of Amaltari, the religious tourism of Maulakalika, the jungle safari in Sauraha, and the natural beauty and hospitality services of Meghauli and Nawalpur.

Nepal–India Cross-Border Tourism Connect 2026 was organized with the support of the private sector and tourism entrepreneurs.(RSS)

title: Cyclone Arnab’s remnants raise landslide risk on Nepal’s main highways - The Kathmandu Post
description: Cyclone Arnab’s remnants raise landslide risk on Nepal’s main highways  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal’s authorities have warned of increased landslide and flood risks along several major highways over the next few days as the remnants of Cyclone Arnab bring rain to parts of the country.

The Flood Forecasting Division and the River and Water Induced Disaster Management Division issued a preliminary landslide risk assessment and early warning on Thursday, identifying vulnerable highway sections in the Narayani, Bagmati and Koshi river basins and surrounding areas.

The warning comes after Cyclone Arnab made landfall along India’s Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday, bringing strong winds and heavy rain. The storm has since weakened into a deep depression, but its residual weather system is expected to bring further rainfall as it moves inland.

The authorities warned that hilly terrain and steep slopes could be particularly vulnerable to landslides and falling rocks. Roads running alongside rivers could face flooding and erosion as water levels rise, while heavy flows in smaller streams and through roadside culverts could damage roads.

The assessment identifies the Narayanghat-Muglin highway, which runs alongside the Trishuli and Narayani rivers, as a risk area. Vulnerable sections of the Koshi and Siddhartha highways have also been flagged, along with the Kanti and Araniko highways and roads connected to the Bagmati river basin.

Other highway sections with a history of landslides or those running close to rivers are also considered vulnerable.

Landslides and floods could block roads and disrupt transport, including the movement of essential supplies, the warning said. The notice outlines potential hazards but does not report any confirmed road closures.

The authorities have urged the public to avoid travelling on highways during rainfall unless necessary. Those who must travel have been advised to check updates from traffic police and road authorities before setting out.

The warnings follow the cyclone’s passage across India’s eastern coast. The India Meteorological Department said Arnab crossed the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts on Wednesday with sustained winds of 125-135 kph and gusts of up to 150 kph before weakening as it moved inland.

Although the risk of similarly strong winds in Nepal is expected to be lower as the system weakens, rain and snowfall remain possible. Authorities have urged trekkers and mountaineers to check official weather forecasts before travelling.

The Department of Tourism, Nepal Tourism Board and Nepal Mountaineering Association have advised tourists and climbing teams to review updated forecasts before undertaking trekking or mountaineering trips.

Nepal’s Civil Aviation Authority has also directed airports and relevant agencies to prepare for possible weather-related disruption, including by reviewing flight plans, runway inspections, air traffic management and communications and power systems.

title: World Stroke Day: More than 50,000 people suffer strokes in Nepal annually - OnlineKhabar English News
description: World Stroke Day: More than 50,000 people suffer strokes in Nepal annually  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Kathmandu, October 29

More than 50,000 people suffer strokes every year in Nepal, according to Dr Raju Poudel, outgoing president of the Nepal Stroke Association.

Poudel shared the figure in an interview on the occasion of World Stroke Day, which is being observed in Nepal today under the slogan “Every Minute Counts”. He said one person suffers a stroke every 10 minutes in the country.

“A stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked. The resulting lack of oxygen and nutrients can cause brain cells to die,” he said.

Established in 2017, the Nepal Stroke Association has been working to assess the prevalence of stroke in Nepal and promote measures for its treatment. The association has been collaborating with University Hospital Heidelberg in Germany to improve stroke treatment in line with international standards. It has also been working on stroke-related issues in collaboration with GIZ and the World Health Organization.

Poudel said one-third of people who suffer a stroke die from it and stressed the need for greater government attention to prevention. He added that one in four people worldwide would experience a stroke during their lifetime, while a stroke occurs somewhere in the world every three seconds.

Around 12 million people worldwide suffer strokes each year, according to the figures cited in the report. Poudel said the government should prioritise stroke prevention and treatment, particularly in least-developed and developing countries such as Nepal.

He said 15–20 per cent of stroke patients in Nepal die from the condition. High blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity and an unbalanced diet are among the risk factors for stroke.

title: Mountain safety experts gather in Nepal as global mountaineering assembly begins - Everest Chronicle
description: Mountain safety experts gather in Nepal as global mountaineering assembly begins  Everest Chronicle
publisher.title: Everest Chronicle
full_article:
More than 60 mountaineers, doctors, rescuers and other specialists from several countries gathered in Nepal for a mountain safety symposium that concluded on Wednesday, with practical training focused on improving safety in high-altitude environments.

The two-day International Mountain Safety Symposium brought together mountain medicine professionals, paramedics, insurance representatives and rescue specialists to exchange expertise and strengthen international cooperation.

On the second day, participants took part in practical demonstrations and field-based training at Scout premises in Kakani, in Nuwakot district, north of Kathmandu.

The programme covered mountain medicine, acclimatisation, altitude-related illnesses, hypothermia, frostbite, expedition preparedness and rescue operations, according to organisers.

The symposium was held ahead of the 2026 General Assembly of the International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation (UIAA), which Nepal is hosting on October 30-31.

The Nepal Mountaineering Association (NMA), the country's national mountaineering body, is hosting the international gathering, which brings together representatives of the global mountaineering community for discussions on mountain safety, environmental protection and climate change.

The assembly's programme also includes a climate change summit on October 31 and discussions on sustainable mountain tourism and the future of Himalayan mountaineering.

Participants are also revisiting the 1982 Kathmandu Declaration on Mountain Protection, which highlighted the international mountaineering community's longstanding interest in protecting mountain environments.

The gathering comes as Nepal seeks to strengthen its role in international mountaineering, drawing on its experience in high-altitude climbing, rescue and mountain tourism.

Kathmandu, October 29 — The United States will provide Nepal with more than $150 million worth of American-made helicopters, drones and riverboats to strengthen the country’s disaster preparedness and response capabilities, the US Embassy in Kathmandu said.

According to a statement issued by the embassy, Chargé d’Affaires, a.i. Megan Bouldin met with Nepali Army Chief of the Army Staff General Ashok Raj Sigdel on Thursday to discuss the strong US-Nepal partnership and ongoing American assistance to help Nepal recover from the devastating floods in August.

During the meeting, Bouldin expressed her deepest condolences to those who lost their lives in the disaster and extended her sympathies to the families of missing Nepali Army personnel.

She also highlighted US assistance aimed at enhancing Nepal’s capacity to respond to natural disasters and other emergencies. The planned delivery of helicopters, drones and riverboats will provide additional resources for search and rescue operations, medical evacuations and emergency response.

The deliveries are scheduled to begin next year, according to the embassy.

The new assistance will build on the $38 million worth of M28 Skytruck aircraft donated by the United States last fall, which have supported relief operations in Nepal.

The embassy said American technology, equipment and expertise are helping Nepal strengthen its disaster-response capabilities, save lives and support communities affected by crises.

The assistance underscores the continued cooperation between the United States and Nepal in disaster preparedness, humanitarian response and emergency management.

title: Nepal urges stronger global climate action - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal urges stronger global climate action  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter, Kathmandu, Oct. 29: Minister for Foreign Affairs Shisir Khanal has called for stronger global climate action, highlighting the need for increased climate finance, support for loss and damage and greater international attention to mountain vulnerabilities as Nepal faces billions of dollars in reconstruction costs following devastating floods and landslides.

Addressing the National Climate Summit 2026 organised ahead of Conference of Parties (COP 31), which is scheduled to take place in Antalya, Turkiye from November 9 to November 20, 2026, Minister Khanal said that the devastating flood of August 26 inflicted immense human suffering and extensive damage upon Nepal's infrastructure, livelihoods, and economy.

“Preliminary assessments indicated that reconstruction and recovery from the August catastrophe alone will require approximately US$ 4.7 billion, equivalent to nearly ten percent of our national GDP,” he said.

Behind these staggering figures lie families mourning their loved ones, communities struggling to rebuild, and decades of hard-earned development gains placed in jeopardy.

“Earlier this month, at the Pre-COP Leaders’ Event in Fiji, I had the opportunity to convey Nepal’s urgent call for global climate action and highlight four priorities that must guide our collective engagement at COP31,” Minister Khanal said.

Nepal has consistently championed mountain concerns through the International Expert Dialogue on Mountains, People and Climate Change in 2024 and the Sagarmatha Sambaad in 2025. We look forward to carrying this momentum into the next Sagarmatha Sambaad in 2027, he said.

“At COP31, we will advocate for regular high-level dialogues on mountains, a dedicated mountain work programme, and the systematic integration of mountain-specific vulnerabilities into global climate frameworks,” Minister Dr. Khanal said.

The recent decision of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage to provisionally allocate US$ 20 million, which marks a milestone in international climate cooperation, with Nepal becoming the first country to secure such an allocation.

Nepal will continue advocating for predictable, grant-based resources and effective rapid-response mechanisms to support recovery and resilient reconstruction.

Minister Khanal said that climate finance must be accessible, equitable and responsive to national priorities. Nepal has demonstrated its commitment through its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDCs), National Adaptation Plan and long-term low-emission development strategy, he said.

“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs remains committed to advancing our national priorities through bilateral diplomacy, regional partnerships, and multilateral cooperation. To anchor this work, the Ministry has established a dedicated Climate Diplomacy Section,” he said

Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Geeta Chaudhary speaking at the National Climate Summit 2026. Photo: Indira Aryal/TRN

Speaking at the event, Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Geeta Chaudhary said that climate justice must not remain limited to words in international documents but be translated into action. “Those who have contributed the least to the climate crisis are suffering its worst consequences. The question of climate justice arises from this very injustice,” she said.

“Climate justice should not remain merely a beautiful phrase in United Nations documents. It must be translated into action,” she said, adding that responsibility for protecting the Himalayas and addressing the impacts of floods must be shared internationally.

Chaudhary also stressed the need to place women, children, young people, senior citizens, Indigenous Peoples and marginalised communities at the centre of climate policy and decision-making, as they often bear a disproportionate share of climate-related losses.

Climate change is not the responsibility of a single ministry or level of government, she said, emphasising the need for coordination among federal, provincial and local governments. Climate adaptation must begin not only at Singha Durbar but also at wards and community levels. Local Adaptation Plans for Action (LAPA) and related local plans should therefore be strengthened and implemented.

Ahead of COP31, she said Nepal would continue to advocate for climate justice, the mountain agenda, adaptation, easier access to climate finance and the effective operation of the loss and damage fund.

The government is preparing documents to present in the upcoming COP31. During the programme, Dr. Maheshwar Dhakal, spokesperson and Chief at the Climate Change Section at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment presented the roadmap to COP31 Kathmandu to Antalaya.

Dr. Dhakal presented position paper to COP 31. The Mountain agenda is one of the key priorities, with a particular focus on addressing the risks of global warming exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius in mountain regions.

According to him, other major priorities include climate change adaptation, loss and damage and securing financial support for communities affected by climate-induced disasters. The agenda also stressed predictable climate finance, technology development and transfer, and carbon market mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

Another priority is strengthening climate change mitigation, transparency, Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and the global stocktake are also among the priorities. Agriculture, food security, health and a just transition have been identified as important areas of action

Likewise, the agenda also highlights inclusive climate justice, with an emphasis on gender equality and the participation of children, young people, persons with disabilities, Indigenous Peoples, sexual and gender minorities, and other vulnerable communities. International cooperation is considered essential to addressing the growing impacts of climate change.
